The first mention of this prayer being employed in its best-known context comes from the 13th century text entitled Or Zarua, and its earliest version is sometimes called the "half" version. Under certain circumstances, a chazzan may recite the "half" variety following a Torah reading, and its "rabbinical" version is recited by those studying the midrash or aggada. Its "Great" version contains a prayer for the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the Temple, and the full version adds two sentences which begin, respectively, "Yohei shlomo rabba" and "Oseh shalom." This prayer, whose purpose is sometimes confused with the prayer "El Molai Rachamim." opens with the line "yit'gadal v'yit'kadash sh'mei raba," and a variant of it is recited by mourners after the death of a loved one. Identify this Jewish prayer extolling the coming kingdom of God.

Michael Sattler authored this group's first declaration of faith, a collection of seven articles known as the "Brotherly Union." According to letters of Conrad Grebel, the Lord's Supper was a sign of love among believers, the church was meant to be a suffering church, and Matthew 18:15 through 18 indicated the importance of witnessing to this denomination, whose early history was told by Thieleman J. Van Braght in the Martyrs Mirror. An offshoot of this denomination developed in Moravia under Jakob Hutter, but their more famous leaders included John of Leiden and Menno Simons, who gave his name to another branch of this denomination, the Mennonites. FTP, identify this religious denomination which held that infants are not punishable for sin and thus emphasized adult baptism.

Controversy embroiled a minister of this religion named James Nayler when he entered the city of Bristol in imitation of Christ's entry into Jerusalem. This religion's preacher Elias Hicks discounted the divine nature of Christ, proposing instead that Christ had achieved divinity through complete obedience to the Inner Light possessed by all men. Founded by George Fox, FTP, name this Christian sect whose members included William Penn and whose nickname refers to their practice of trembling during prayer.

The epigraph to this book comes from the book of Romans and reads "Vengeance is mine: I will repay,' saith the Lord". The protagonist of this work arrives in its opening setting solely to attempt to settle a dispute between her brother and Dolly. The title character sometimes sneaks into town to see her son, Seryagov, but has little interest in her illegitimate daughter. At the end of this work, the title character throws herself in front of a train, and Levin and Kitty work together to build a happy life, while Vronsky is already dead. Famously beginning "Happy families are all alike, but all unhappy families are unhappy in their own way", identify this work by Leo Tolstoy.

A traditional greeting said on this holiday is "L'shanah tovah tikatev v'taihatem." One of the festivities associated with this holiday consists of teruah and tekiah and is not observed if it falls on Shabbat, and tashlikh may also be observed by crossing a river or other flowing water. One ritual associated with this observance is described in Numbers 29:1, and involves blowing a shofar, or ram's horn. Another ritual involved in this holiday is marked with 10 days of introspection, which may have led to this holiday's nickname "Day of Judgement". Identify this holiday celebrated on Tishrei 1 and 2, the traditional Jewish New Year.

Some scriptural evidence for this doctrine may be found in Genesis 3:15, which holds that God put enmity between the subject of this doctrine and the Serpent, and also in Luke 1:28, in which the phrase kecharitomene implies the pre-existence of this condition. Some scholars have drawn comparison between Eve and the subject of this doctrine to justify it. Pius IX promulgated this doctrine in the Ineffabilis Deus in 1854, and on the anniversary of this, there is a feast; specifically, on December 8th. Identify this Catholic doctrine, which holds that Mary must have been free from original sin in order to have conceived Jesus.

At the end of this writing, Yahweh signifies his acceptance of the Jews as his people by covering their tent with his cloud, and earlier, through the prayers of their leader, they defeated Amalec. At the site of a calf made of gold, one figure in this book breaks some tablets, and a pillar of clouds and fire protects the Israelites. Early in this book, Pharaoh's heart is unwilling to move in the face of nine plagues, and later, God provides manna from heaven and the Decalogue on top of a mountain. Identify this book of the Pentateuch, which deals with 40 years of wandering in the Desert of Sin and comes directly after Genesis in the Bible.

This Biblical book contains advice against kicking one's husband's opponent in the groin or wearing cloth of mixed fibers. This advice and other mitzvot appear in its second section, a discourse on how the Israelites should act while living in Canaan, and the end of this book sees a short appendix which details the final blessings and death of Moses. The most notable part of this book, however, is the "Shema Yisrael," which has been adopted as the basic credo of Judaism. Consisting of three sermons by Moses, name this fifth book of the Old Testament, which follows Numbers and precedes Judges.

In Islam, these people can practice "zuhd," and one group of them is known as the Sanusiyah, which manufactures perfume. In Buddhism, the status of mahathera is a possible honor for some of them, who undergo the upasampada procedure to become a bhikku and follow the vinaya. In Christianity, almost all of these people practice cenobitism, and their lifestyle was founded by Pacomius of the Thebeiad and Anthony of Egypt. The Benedictine Rule guides what cloistered individuals, who devote themselves to religion apart from the world?

Important texts for this group include the Record of Talks on the Law and the Poisonous Stamens and Pistils of Thorns, written by Hakuin. Its members created chinzo portraits and bokuseki calligraphy, and it included a late denomination that believed in the chanting called nembutsu. The goal in this sect is to achieve satori, whether through sitting, as in the Soto group, or verbal methods, as in Rinzai. Brought to China by Bodhidharma and Japan by Dogen, it makes use of statements which may equate the Buddha with three pounds of flax, known as koans. Name this anti-rational form of Buddhism.

In the Jewish liturgical year, it encompasses the parshas of Shemini, Tzav, and Vayikra. This book explains that the showbread is to be laid out in two rows of six loaves and contains instructions on the ritual of killing a scapegoat for Azazel. Chapter 25, verse 10 of it is inscribed on the Liberty Bell, and this book also includes the episode in which Nadab and Abihu bring "strange fire" to the Tabernacle. It explains the ritual for purifying a leper, lists clean and unclean animals, and includes the Priestly Code, which is why it is named for the priestly tribe. Identify this third book of the Old Testament, found between Exodus and Numbers.

This religious group is based on a set of sutras telling of the vows the monk Dharmākara made prior to his ascension to buddhahood, especially his 18th vow. It was transmitted from China to Japan by Hōnen, whose disciple Shinran expressed this school's final conclusion that enlightenment could only be achieved by faith in the grace of Dharmākara under his new name as a Buddha. Along with Chan or Zen, it is the most popular variant of Mahayana Buddhism in East Asia. Name this school that focuses on the recitation of the Amitābha, or Amida Buddha's name, to achieve entry into its namesake heavenly realm.

Principally rooted in the old religions of Europe, this religion is a spiritual way of life which celebrates the belief that each person should find his or her spirituality according to the dictates of the inner voice of their own soul. It honors the Divine in all of its aspects, perceiving it within each person's own experience. Members of this religion believe in seeking spiritual union with Divinity by exploring their inner selves and attuning to nature. FTP name this faith which includes such traditions as shamanism and wicca.

This congregational clergyman born in England asserted the freedom of the individual to make their own decisions in politics and religion. He was educated at Cambridge and his doctrines were so strongly opposed by Archbishop Laud, that Laud planned to have him silenced, so he fled to Holland. He stayed there for 3 years until he and his congregation could emigrate to Newtown, Massachusetts. Called "the most powerful pulpit orator among the ministers of New England", he would later move his congregation to Connecticut. FTP name this man who founded Hartford and who helped write and get passed the Fundamental Orders in his colony of Connecticut.

Three characters alienated from modern society, Claire, Andy, and Dag, take up residence in Palm Springs; they have been taken by many cultural observers to symbolize the ennui common to The book's title, derived from the last chapter of Paul Fussell's sociological work 'Class,' has become a popular buzzword to refer to a large subgroup of Americans. FTP identify this 1991 work of Douglas Coupland.

Their beliefs were set forth in Twelve Conclusions: condemnation of the papacy; belief in the primacy of the Scriptures; and condemnation of sacramentals, confession, pilgrimages, and other practices of the Catholic Church. Persecuted beginning in 1399 by Henry IV, their founder was known as the "Morning Star of the Reformation." FTP name these Oxford-based reformer who followed John Wycliffe.

This man believed that virginity was the ideal state, even greater than celibacy. He asserted the Church's autonomy in a series of debates with Symmachus, and his feud with Theodosius led him to temporarily deprive the emperor of the sacraments. FTP name this Byzantine theologian and bishop of Milan.

Until the 17th century he was thought to be a contemporary of Moses, and his writings were considered almost as sacred as the Bible. Actually, the books ascribed to him were written by a group of teachers who lived in Alexandria in the first two centuries BC or AD. Still, his supposed writings on alchemy and the occult had influence on the French symbolists and William Butler Yeats. FTP give the name sometimes applied to the Egyptian god Thoth-- the source of Hermeticism.

Chapter 22, verse 5 of this book proscribes the wearing of men's clothes by women, while chapter four describes the destruction of the followers of Baalpeor and of Sihon of Heshbon. Chapter two notes that Zamzummims, or giants, once existed among the children of Ammon, but God killed them all, and it warns the Israelites not to harm the Ammonites. The fourth verse of its sixth chapter states, "Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our god, the Lord is one," which constitutes the Shema. With a name derived from the Greek for "second law," FTP what is this fifth book of the Old Testament?

Celebration of this observance by adherents in Iran includes the kiddush levana, or blessing of the moon, and on it pregnant women offer two hens to the schochet for killing. Instituted by Leviticus 23:26 et passim, common observance includes a reading from Jonah, and it features the Shimon Edrei, or communal confession of sins. Its prohibitions include the wearing of cosmetics or leather, and it begins with the evening prayer known as Kol Nidre. Ending with the blowing of the tekiah gedolah on the shofar. FTP what is this tenth of Tishri holiday, the Jewish "Day of Atonement"?

Brahmacharya, meaning celibacy, is practiced by monks and nuns of this religion. Other practices include Aparigraha, complete asceticism and the idea of Satya, or ultimate truth. One of its two primary sects believes that women cannot achieve moksha, while the other does, but not much else but the wearing of clothes separates the Digambara and Svetembara. Practicing vegetarianism as part of its adherence to Ahimsa is, FTP, what Indian religion founded by Mahavira?

The 17th of September is the feast day of this concept in Catholicism, commemorating its occurrence at the mountain retreat of La Verna in 1224 on a noted saint. One common thread in all occurrences is the lack of an associated fetid odor, and that of Juana of the Cross and some others actually gave the smell of perfume, a scent known as the "odor of sanctity." When it was visited on Catherine of Siena, she showed humility by praying for it to be hidden. Comprising the visible evidence of wounds or invisible pain associated with them, FTP what is this manifestation of Christ's wounds on ecstatic followers?

Companions of this figure include Little Merry, a cook; Shanty Boy, a singer; Johnny Inkslinger, his chronicler; and Hot Biscuit Slim. One account suggests he had seven assistants, all named "Elmer," all of whom were able to wrap their beards around themselves for warmth. Folklorist Richard Dorson coined the term "fakelore" in writings about this figure, suggesting that much of his history does not come from a true oral tradition, like the tale of his dragging of a pick-axe creating the Grand Canyon or his digging of Lake Michigan as a drinking bowl for his enormous pet. Originating in logging tales in Canada and Michigan, FTP name this enormous axe man, friend of the Blue Ox, Babe.

One form of this practice involves a framework analyzing Activating Events, beliefs, and Consequences, named the ABC framework. That practice, developed by Albert Ellis, is part of a broader category of this that includes Joseph Wolpe's systematic desensitization. The rational-emotive type of this is part of the behavioral class of this practice, which can be used to remove stutters. Alcoholics Anonymous is an example of this practice for groups. Name this general term denoting psychologists' work with patients to help treat their disorders.

In one section of this text, a figure's life is threatened after he is mistaken for someone who wronged the people of K'uang, though that figure claims since "heaven has not allowed finesse to perish," nothing can happen to him. Wang notes that the Heijan and Qi-Lu versions of this text were recovered by King Gong of Lu, and those versions were redacted into the Marquis Zhang version, the standard version probably compiled by the students of Zhangzi. It contains such sections as "Studying" and Li Ren, or "living in brotherliness," and notes that "The Master's enquiry is different from that of the others." FTP name this one of the Four Books, written during the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history, comprising the collected sayings and subsequent discussions of Confucius and his disciples.

This book's fortieth chapter provided the aria "O thou that tellest good tidings to Zion." That chapter begins with a description of a road from Persia and prophesies that "every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill made low" in order to build it. This scripture's second part is sometimes called the "Book of Comfort;" its first part prophesies that the nations persecuting Judah will be defeated, but also warns the people that they have broken the covenant of God by worshipping idols. Identify this book of the Old Testament foretelling the glory of Zion and written by a prophet who was later sawed in half.

This person's attitude towards religion was embodied in the "dual principle" of his advisor Phagspa, who persuaded him to make Tibet autonomous. He divided society into "semu jen," "han jen," and "man tzu" classes and sent armies to destroy the kingdom of Pagan at the Battle of Ngasaunggyan. He came to power after brief strife with his brother Arigböge. At the kuriltai of 1260, he succeeded Möngke as great Khan, but that did not enable his fleets to overcome the "kamikaze" winds around Japan. Name this grandson of Genghis who established the Yuan Dynasty in China and entertained Marco Polo.

This man had chosen for himself the rich land of the Jordan upon which he raised his herds, so that his herdsmen would not quarrel with a certain individual's. While living in the mountains near Zoar, this man's daughters got him drunk on two separate occasions so he would impregnate them, and their descendants became the Moabites and the Ammonites. When the kings Chedorlaomer, Tidal, Amraphel, and Arioch captured him and his possessions, Abram armed his servants and pursued them to Hobah, rescuing him. Name this man who lived in Sodom and whose wife was turned to a pillar of salt.

This figure's wife was accused of being Ethiopian by his siblings, after which his sister was stricken with leprosy for seven days. He gained that wife by defeating some shepherds at a well, thus defending the honor of the daughters of the Midianite Jethro. His son Gershom was sent home along with Zipporah when the angel of death came down. His sister was Miriam and his brother, owner of a blooming staff, was Aaron. Name this Hebrew who paved the way for his people through the Red Sea.

This character returns to his youthful religion just before the end of his life, as we are told he says a prayer in Hebrew. Earlier, this lover of "making handkerchiefs" had a would-be defector from his organization brought before him so he can relate the tale of a previous "peach." Eventually winding up in Newgate, this classmate of Bill Sykes is visited by the title character of the work in which he appears shortly before his hanging. Name this employer of Charley Bates and Jack Dawkins, the Artful Dodger; the villainous head of a gang of youthful pickpockets in Dickens' Oliver Twist.

Presently, its highest ranking official is Albert Lincoln, who addressed the community in June 2006 regarding its places of worship in Israel as possible Hezbollah targets. Its first House of Worship was completed in Ashkhabad, Russia, and Shoghi Effendi compiled the writings of this religion's founders and early leaders in its most holy scripture, the Kitab-i-Aqdas. Identify this religion founded in Persia, whose followers consider the Bab among its forerunners.

A common belief of members of this group holds that life is "joyous" though it has a "maggoty" center. One sect of these people believe that a vampire named Yara-Ma-Yha-Who jumped out of a fig tree and gobbled up people, spitting them out slightly shorter but no worse for wear. A "Rainbow Serpent" that inhabits water holes is one creator god of this people, and is sometimes associated with the female snake Einaga. Their tradition holds that the preceding age is known as the Alcheringa. This group believes in fairies called Mimi from Arnhem land, and their tradition holds that the world was created during the Dreamtime. Name this group that holds Uluru, or Ayers Rock, to be sacred.

Extras One legend states that, on this holiday, one could throw a ninth of an apple over one's shoulder to obtain the answer to a question. Celebrants of this holiday put extra chairs around their tables to welcome the influence of spirits, though at other times, they practice transvestitism to fool the spirits into thinking that they are other people. One celebration of this holiday involves sticking one's head in a tub of apples and attempting to remove them with one's mouth; that bobbing is meant to commemorate the tree in the middle of Emhain Abhlach. Situated opposite Beltrane on the calendar, FTP, name this Pagan harvest holiday celebrated on November 1, which means "Summer's End."

In Surah 34 of the Quran, Allah grants this figure command of the winds, which allows this figure to complete a two-month journey in one day. This figure banished Abiathar to Ananoth after Abiathar sided with this man's brother Adonijah. Towards the end of his life, this ruler's gentile wives convinced him to worship Asteroth and Milcom which led Ahijah of Shiloh to predict the fracturing of this man's kingdom. At this wishes of his father, this man killed off Joab in the Tabernacle. He was succeeded by his son Rehoboam who later lost the control of ten tribes to Jereboam. This man's most famous construction project featured cedar from Tyre and was intended as a permanent home for the Ark of the Covenant, and he was once visited by the Queen of Sheba. FTP, name this Israelite king who constructed the first Temple and once ordered the halving of a baby, the second son of Bathsheba and David.

This author outlined his views on religion in works like "The Human Abode of the Religious Function" and A Common Faith. This philosopher argued that knowledge is obtained from active interaction with an organism's environment in his article "The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology." In addition to arguing that the state arose out of subsequently larger local organizations in one work, this philosopher argued that public habits must be cultivated early in life. He outlined his views on aesthetics in Art and Experience, and in his most famous work, this philosopher defined the title subject as the "social continuity of life" and argued that it should be structured with experimentation to prepare children for a creative life. Identify this philosopher who wrote The School and Society and Democracy and Education, an American Pragmatist.

The Sonnini Manuscript purports to be a lost chapter of this book and makes the dubious claim that Roman Britain was inhabited by Jews. One figure in this book throws the viper into the fire while suffering no harm, which causes him to be called a god. The orator Tertullus serves as a prosecutor in this text, as do people described as "the Cyrenians." Ananias and Sapphira die in this book after lying about their income. This book sees Tabitha raised from the dead, as well as the election of St. Matthias to replace a man who had accepted thirty pieces of silver. Name this book of the Bible that describes the deeds of Jesus's followers.

Eicha and kinnot are chanted during this holiday, which comes at the end of a three-week preparation period during which activities including weddings, haircuts, and purchasing clothing are forbidden. Traditionally, tefillin cannot be used until late in the day of this holiday, and figures involved in this observance include ten scouts of Moses and Bar Kokhba. Only depressing texts are allowed to be studied on this day, which also commemorates the destruction of the two temples. Identify this Jewish holiday which observes a litany of sad events that happened on the namesake day of the Jewish calendar.
